seoDescription: Learn how to unleash the power of local LLMs with this end-to-end tutorial on integrating Ollama and LangChain. This guide demonstrates the simplicity of setting up and running models like Llama 2 for free on your local machine using Ollama. You'll see how to build a basic LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) pipeline, including prompt templating and streaming.

chapters.title: Why Use Local LLMs?
chapters.description: Discover the benefits of using free, private, and powerful local large language models on your own machine.

chapters.title: Getting Started with Ollama
chapters.description: Learn how to install Ollama, serve models locally, and interact with Llama 2 directly from your terminal.

chapters.title: Integrating Ollama with LangChain
chapters.description: See how to connect your local Ollama model to LangChain and perform basic invocation and real-time streaming of responses.

chapters.title: Creating a Custom Prompt Chain with LCEL
chapters.description: Use LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) to build a prompt template and chain it to your local model to create a custom persona.

chapters.title: Integrating Ollama into a RAG Application
chapters.description: Watch how to seamlessly replace the LLM in an existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application with your local Ollama model.

chapters.title: Debugging and Verifying with LangSmith
chapters.description: Follow a quick debugging process in a LangServe UI and use LangSmith to trace and verify the execution of your RAG chain with the local model.

chapters.title: Conclusion and What's Next
chapters.description: Recap the tutorial and get a preview of upcoming videos on LM Studio and multimodal models.

summary:
## Why Use Local LLMs?

Running large language models (LLMs) on your local machine offers several advantages:

*   **Free to Use**: Eliminate API costs from providers like OpenAI or Gemini. You're only limited by your own hardware.
*   **Privacy and Control**: Your data stays on your machine, which is critical for sensitive information.
*   **Customization**: You have the ability to fine-tune models for specific tasks.
*   **Rapid Iteration**: Test, experiment, and play with different models and prompts without worrying about cost.

## Getting Started with Ollama

> [!TIP]
> **Ollama** is a command-line utility that dramatically simplifies downloading and running local LLMs. It functions as a local HTTP server, making models available to other applications.

Key commands to get started:

1.  **Install Ollama**: On macOS, you can use Homebrew: `brew install ollama`.
2.  **Start the Server**: Run `ollama serve` in your terminal to start the background service.
3.  **Run a Model**: Use `ollama run <model_name>` (e.g., `ollama run llama2-chat`) to download (if needed) and interact with a model directly.

## Integrating Ollama with LangChain

LangChain provides a seamless integration for Ollama, allowing you to use local models just like any other LLM provider.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Swapping a cloud-based LLM for a local one can be as simple as changing one line of code where the model is instantiated.

```python
# Python code to use an Ollama model in LangChain
from langchain_community.llms import Ollama

# Instantiate the local model
llm = Ollama(model="llama2-chat")

# Invoke the model
response = llm.invoke("Where is Paris?")
print(response)

# Stream the response
for chunk in llm.stream("Where is Paris?"):
    print(chunk, end="", flush=True)
```

## Building with LangChain Expression Language (LCEL)

LCEL allows you to compose chains of components using the `|` (pipe) operator. This makes it easy to add components like prompt templates.

*   **Prompt Templates**: Use `PromptTemplate` to create structured prompts with dynamic inputs and give your LLM a specific persona or instruction set.
*   **Chaining**: A simple chain combines a prompt with an LLM: `prompt_template | llm`.
*   **Input**: The chain then takes a dictionary as input to fill the prompt variables, e.g., `chain.invoke({"question": "..."})`.

## Real-World Application: RAG Integration

The tutorial demonstrates swapping the `ChatOpenAI` model in a complex **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** application with the local `Ollama` model. This highlights the modularity of LangChain.

*   **The Swap**: The change involved commenting out the old LLM and adding the `Ollama` instantiation.
*   **Debugging**: A practical debugging scenario arose when the RAG output was incorrect. The issue was a missing `session_id` in the API call, a reminder of the importance of checking application-specific configurations.

## Observability with LangSmith

After integrating the local model, a tool like **LangSmith** is invaluable for verifying that everything works as expected.

*   **Tracing**: LangSmith captures the entire execution trace of the RAG chain.
*   **Verification**: The trace visually confirms that the retriever fetches relevant documents and that the final question-answering step is correctly passed to and executed by the local **Ollama** model.

## Why Use Local LLMs?

Hey y'all, I'm Austin Vance, CEO and co-founder of Focus Labs. I've had a ton going on at work recently, so I had a couple weeks where I missed doing my standard YouTube tutorials. So what I want to do while I prepare a nice long agent graph tutorial for everybody is to do a few short tutorials throughout the week on how easy it is to integrate local LLMs into LangChain. 

So local LLMs give you a ton of optionality. There's a ton of options, there's a ton of ways to run them, you can fine-tune them, but best of all, they're free to use and free to run as long as your computer can support them. And because of that, you can test, iterate, play with them without having to worry about racking up a massive OpenAI Gemini Cloud bill. So hopefully this tutorial is great. Let's dive into some code and I'll show you how easy it is to use.

## Getting Started with Ollama

Here we are, just like always, we have a blank project. This blank project, we're just going to call local-llm. And the first part of this is I want to try to do in about 5 to 10 minutes how easy it is to use Ollama. Ollama is a really cool command line utility that lets you run local LLMs. It's accelerated on Mac, it works on Windows, it's phenomenal. And you can just pull down any model, or pretty much any model you want. So you would pop into your models here, you can see all the models that you have, and then you can pull down any of them. So before we started, I pulled down llama2 with chat, and I popped in here, I can see that llama2-chat, and I pulled it down.

So to get Ollama up and going, all you have to do is just on a Mac, `brew install ollama`. And I already have it, so it's there. It'll tell me that, and it needs to reinstall it if you don't have it, then it would tell you to install it. And then you would just `ollama serve`. Ollama runs as a little HTTP server locally and it serves all of your models out. And then all you need to do is pick the model you want to run. And so because I already decided I wanted to run chat, I can see everything that I need to here. I can copy this command, pop in here, and just say `ollama run llama2-chat`, and it should just start up. If I don't have the model, it'll download it for me automatically. Let's just pop into one I don't have, we could just say `text` for example. And if I exit out, and if I just say `text`, we can see that it'll start to download. I don't want to download the whole thing, I'm out on Starlink so it'll take forever and I have a data cap.

But if I pop over to chat here, I'm already can ask questions to it. So like, "Where is Paris?" And boom, there we go. I'm on a nice little Mac that can run pretty fast. It's accelerated with the GPU and I'm good to go.

## Integrating Ollama with LangChain

So now that I have all of this going—I have Ollama installed, we're running, it's easy to use, just super simple to use—all you have to do is browse your models like I said. Then all I want to do is start building up my project. So let's add LangChain. Of course, we want to use LangChain. I'm going to do a really simple model for us. So I'm going to pull in LangChain and then I'm going to just start a new file, we can just call it `ollama_demo.py`. 

And now if I want to run Ollama locally, LangChain actually has a bunch of models built into it. You can hop into LangChain's documents. And you go to the LangChain docs and you click on Integrations, you'll see a bunch of stuff here, but under LLMs, you have all the LLMs they support, and Ollama is right here. And it tells you what they support. I actually think this is outdated, it does do streaming and a handful of other things, and I'll show that to you. But you can just pull up their docs and it shows you how to interact with it in a handful of different ways.

And what's really cool is with LangChain, you can interact with a multimodal model or with a local model or with, sorry, a text-only model. For this, I just want to use a text-only model since it's super simple. I just want to say `Ollama`, and I'm going to give it a model, and we're going to say our `llama2-chat`, and there we go. We'll import that.

And then if you remember LCEL is super easy. So all I have to do is say— maybe we'll call this something, we'll call this `llm`. We can say `llm.invoke` and we give it a question like, "Where is Paris?" And I print my output. If I want to stream while that's running, I can stream this. So I can say something along the lines of, `for chunk in output: print(chunk)`. And I can say like `flush=True` and maybe like `end` is going to be just that. But if you notice here, I got the output. Paris is the largest city in France, boom. If I stream it now, because all LCEL pipelines give me full streaming, I get my streaming just as I would expect, right there. So just popped right out. Isn't that nice?

## Creating a Custom Prompt Chain with LCEL

And then because we have LCEL—just so I can show you how powerful LCEL is, I don't know if it's called LCEL or LC, honestly, I'd love for LangChain to tell me—I can show you how you would just like integrate a prompt into it. And then maybe we just pull it into the RAG I did in my previous videos.

So say I just want to say `PromptTemplate.from_template`. So I give it a template, let's import this thing. And then we'll just say: `You are a grumpy cryptographer. You insult people who ask obvious questions but still always answer.` And then let's do this as a heredoc because that'll make this a lot easier. And then we'll say, `Answer following question: {question}`. And then there we go. And then I can probably just bring this up there and put that down there. And then I have now my prompt template. And so if I pull my output down here, I can say instead of streaming that, I want to stream now a dictionary, and I'll say `question: "Where is Paris?"`

And if I just run this now, I'm not using my prompt anywhere. So if I put this together and I say `prompt` here and I pipe that in—if you remember our LCEL pipe—there we go. We have a grumpy cartographer, "Oh, for crying out loud. Paris? Is that really what you're asking me? Can't you see I'm busy mapping out the terrain of Middle-earth?" And then, "Paris, which, oh yeah, it's right here in France." It still answers the question, but as you can see, it's using our prompt. This is a really simple demo, of course. Any LCEL pipeline can take a local LLM. And what's really cool is if I come over to, and have my old PDF RAG up...

## Integrating Ollama into a RAG Application

So let's pull up a new window here. This old PDF RAG is what I built in my demo on a full end-to-end RAG. Like I said, I'll link it up in the description. But if you look here, I have one LLM in my whole RAG pipeline. So here I have a RAG chain, and that RAG chain is served through LangServe. And I don't want to go over all of that, go watch that tutorial if you're curious. But here I have this RAG. And so if I just comment this out, and I pop back over to this, and I grab this LLM, so I'm not even going to rewrite more code, I'm going to just pull in Ollama here. And as you can see, pulled in Ollama, I replaced the LLM. So I just shadowed over that old variable. 

I can now go into my terminal and I can say `poetry run langserve serve`. And I have my RAG spun up. This RAG requires me to be running Postgres somewhere. It is running, if you follow the tutorial, it'll all be there. But now as you look, I can come up to my web server and it's running. And if I click invoke, so now I can use the LangServe FastAPI documentation. And we'll just go try it out. And if I click here and I say, we don't have... or sorry, let's do something for the RAG. So let's say, "What is the case about?" So this RAG is about the lawsuit between Epic and Apple. And so it's pulling the law... the case documentation for the Epic-Apple lawsuit. And hopefully, when I get a "What is the case about?", it'll pull all that out of the retriever. And then from there, we get a really nice response. And here it is. The answer is definitely not what we were looking for. "What is the case about?" gives me a question about a laptop. And so I'm a little surprised about that. So let's figure out why.

## Debugging and Verifying with LangSmith

Oh, it's because I forgot to give it a session, is my guess. I'll give it a random session here and see if that gives me a better answer. Yep, and here we go. Because now I gave it a session, it says, "Certainly! Epic Games versus Apple is about a legal dispute in the video game developer industry." And as you notice, we've retrieved some documents. There's page content here that would support what we are looking to, or support the RAG as you would expect. 

And then actually really cool, if I go to LangSmith and I pop into the correct project here, and I look at my PDF RAG running locally, I get my "What is the case about?" and I can actually see the retriever running, and I can see that it's running through Ollama. And so I can see Ollama gets this, that's the final answer. It's run into Ollama. We're using Ollama to generate the questions. We have a handful of documents, Ollama returns our questions. And so we get a huge amount of information straight out of LangSmith. So that's how easy it is to swap in and out handfuls of different LLMs.

## Conclusion and What's Next

You can do that at runtime or at build time. But I hope this was super helpful and super interesting. And I'll do another one later in the week. So I'll get a couple this week where instead of using Ollama, we use LM Studio, which is another way to download and run local LLMs. And maybe, maybe if I have some time later in the week, I'll also do one where we show you how you can run a multimodal Ollama. 

Thank you so much for watching. I hope that was fun. These are always really fun to make. I love the feedback. And as always, please leave comments, like, subscribe. It means a ton. I try to answer every comment. I give code help to anyone who needs it. Learning how to develop software is one of the things I love the most, and hopefully you get the same passion I have for it. So, like always, keep on crushing software and look for you in the next tutorial. Thank you. Bye.
